# 大语言模型与基础模型在药物系统性评估中的现状与未来：从多组学到个体化模拟

## 1. 引言

传统药物研发长期面临“高投入、长周期、低成功率”的困境。尽管多组学技术（基因组学、转录组学、蛋白质组学、代谢组学等）的进步为理解药物作用机制提供了前所未有的数据维度，但单一组学或简单联用仍难以系统、宏观地解析药物对机体产生的整体影响。更关键的是，个体间的异质性——包括遗传背景、表观遗传状态、环境暴露、微生物组差异等——使得群体平均水平的药物反应预测在临床实践中往往失效。

近年来，以大型语言模型（LLM）和基础模型（Foundation Model）为代表的第三代人工智能技术，正在为这一困境提供全新的解决路径。这些模型不再局限于单一任务或单一数据模态，而是通过在海量、多源生物医学数据上进行预训练，学习到生物系统的深层表征，从而具备模拟药物-机体相互作用、预测个体化药物反应的能力。本报告将系统调研当前阶段大模型在这一领域的应用现状、技术路径、核心挑战以及未来发展方向。

---

## 2. 当前阶段：大模型如何用于药物系统性评估

### 2.1 基础模型在药物研发中的爆发式增长

自2022年以来，应用于药物研发的基础模型数量呈现爆发式增长。截至2025年，已有超过200个基础模型被发表，覆盖靶点发现、分子性质优化、临床前应用等多个环节[1]。这些模型的核心优势在于其“通用性”：通过在大规模、多样化的生物医学数据上进行预训练，它们可以适应多种下游任务，无需针对每个任务从头训练模型。

> **关键事实**：仅2022至2025年间，药物研发领域发表的基础模型数量已超过200个，涵盖靶点发现、分子性质优化、临床前应用等多个环节[1]。
> 
> 来源：https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41167387

### 2.2 药物反应预测：从细胞系到患者的跨越

药物反应预测是精准医学的核心任务之一。传统方法依赖细胞系药物筛选数据，但细胞系与真实患者之间存在显著差异。大模型正在改变这一局面。

**DRPLLM（Drug Response Prediction using Large Language Model）** 是这一方向的代表性工作。该框架将Llama-8B大语言模型与深度神经网络回归头相结合，通过将细胞系基因表达、突变信息和药物性质格式化为自然语言提示，提取嵌入特征进行药物反应预测。在GDSC v2和CCLE数据集上训练后，模型达到了0.71的Spearman秩相关系数（SCC），经超参数优化后提升至0.74。更重要的是，在患者来源异种移植（PDX）队列上的验证显示，基于嵌入的方法（SCC=0.45，p<1e-16）显著优于传统的提示工程方法（SCC=0.06，p>0.05）[2]。

> **关键事实**：DRPLLM框架利用Llama-8B LLM在PDX队列上实现了SCC=0.45的预测性能（p<1e-16），显著优于传统提示工程方法，证明LLM嵌入方法在药物反应预测中的可泛化性[2]。
> 
> 来源：https://mayoclinic.elsevierpure.com/en/publications/drpllm-a-large-language-model-based-framework-for-predicting-drug

**单细胞基础模型**在药物反应预测方面也取得了突破。scFoundation模型基于xTrimoGene Transformer架构，拥有1亿参数，在超过5000万人类单细胞RNA测序数据上训练，能够执行基因表达增强、药物反应预测、单细胞药物反应分类等任务[3]。CPA（Compositional Perturbation Autoencoder）模型则整合了线性模型的可解释性和深度学习的灵活性，可对未见条件下的药物反应进行预测，支持药物相似性分析和跨物种时间序列数据验证[3]。

> **关键事实**：scFoundation（1亿参数，5000万单细胞训练）和CPA等模型可对未见药物条件和遗传扰动进行单细胞水平的反应预测[3]。
> 
> 来源：https://codeocean.com/blog/map-of-foundational-models-for-use-in-biotech-and-pharma-rd

**PERCEPTION** 精准肿瘤学计算管线利用公共可用的大规模细胞系药物筛选数据中的匹配批量细胞和单细胞表达谱，在多发性骨髓瘤、乳腺癌和肺癌患者临床试验中成功预测了对靶向治疗的反应[4]。

> **关键事实**：PERCEPTION管线在多个临床试验中成功预测了患者对靶向治疗的反应，证明单细胞转录组学在个体化药物反应预测中的临床可行性[4]。
> 
> 来源：https://www.nature.com/articles/s41392-026-02631-6

### 2.3 多组学整合：从单一维度到系统生物学

基础模型的核心优势之一在于其能够天然整合多种组学数据，实现从“还原论”到“系统生物学”的范式转变。

**scGPT** 作为首个单细胞基础模型，采用生成式预训练Transformer架构，在来自CELLxGENE Discover的3300万正常人类细胞转录组上训练，覆盖51个器官/组织、441个独立研究。该模型不仅能够进行跨组织细胞类型注释和批次整合，还能实现**多组学数据对齐**（如scRNA-seq/scATAC-seq联合嵌入）、**原位扰动响应预测**（CRISPRi/化学扰动）和**上下文感知的基因调控网络推断**[4]。

> **关键事实**：scGPT在3300万单细胞转录组上预训练，实现了多组学数据对齐（scRNA-seq/scATAC-seq联合嵌入）、原位扰动预测和基因调控网络推断[4]。
> 
> 来源：https://www.nature.com/articles/s41392-026-02631-6

**Pathformer** 模型采用基于通路的稀疏神经网络和十字交叉注意力机制，整合多组学数据进行癌症诊断、预后和药物反应预测，在多个数据集上显著提升了F1分数[3]。

**IBM Research 生物医学基础模型（BMFM）** 技术利用多模态数据，包括药物样小分子、蛋白质（总计超过10亿分子）以及单细胞RNA序列等，提供跨模态的预测能力[5]。

> **关键事实**：IBM BMFM覆盖超过10亿分子和单细胞RNA序列数据，可支持多模态、多领域的预测任务[5]。
> 
> 来源：https://research.ibm.com/projects/biomedical-foundation-models

**多模态LLM框架**进一步扩展了这一范式。通过整合结构化分子谱与非结构化数据源（如生物医学文献、临床记录、影像数据），LLM可以实现上下文感知的预测和假设生成。在肿瘤学中，多模态LLM代理系统已展示出通过融合放射组学、病理学和指南文本提供个性化治疗建议的可行性[6]。

> **关键事实**：多模态LLM框架可整合结构化分子数据与非结构化临床文本，在肿瘤学中已展示出提供个性化治疗推荐的能力[6]。
> 
> 来源：https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12722026

### 2.4 单细胞扰动预测：模拟药物对细胞的影响

准确预测细胞对遗传或化学扰动的反应，是药物发现的核心环节。如果能够精确模拟基因敲除或新药候选物对细胞的影响，就可以更快速地识别治疗靶点并更早地发现潜在副作用。

**Geneformer** 在2800万单细胞转录组上预训练后，利用有限的外部队列（n=1500）实现了稳健的靶点预测。该模型推荐的mTOR抑制剂依维莫司在实验中显示出显著的功能改善：左心室缩短分数增加18.3%，I型胶原沉积减少52%，最大线粒体呼吸能力提升37%[4]。

> **关键事实**：Geneformer在2800万单细胞上预训练后，利用仅1500例患者的外部队列即可实现稳健靶点预测，其推荐的mTOR抑制剂在动物实验中验证了显著疗效[4]。
> 
> 来源：https://www.nature.com/articles/s41392-026-02631-6

**PertEval-scFM** 基准测试框架系统评估了单细胞基础模型在扰动效应预测中的表现，特别关注零样本设置下基础模型嵌入相对于简单基线模型的效果[7]。

**融合模型（Fusion-based model）** 在预测遗传敲除效应方面已接近实验误差极限。在Jurkat和K562细胞系中，基于融合的方法达到了与估计实验误差限相匹配的性能，表明在某些受控条件下，AI模拟已接近理论最优水平[8]。

> **关键事实**：在特定细胞系中，AI融合模型对遗传敲除效应的预测性能已接近实验测量误差极限，证明了AI模拟细胞行为的巨大潜力[8]。
> 
> 来源：https://genbio.ai/foundation-models-improve-perturbation-response-prediction

#### 值得关注的争议

然而，并非所有研究都对基础模型持乐观态度。2024-2025年的多项独立评估（Boiarsky等，2024；Ahlmann-Eltze等，2025）发现，在扰动预测等核心任务上，深度学习方法并未持续优于简单的PCA加线性回归[9][10]。这一发现提示，在模型复杂度提升的同时，需要谨慎评估其边际收益，尤其是在数据规模有限或生物学变异较小时。

> **关键事实**：独立评估显示，在单细胞扰动预测任务中，深层基础模型并不总是优于PCA+线性回归等简单方法，提示该领域仍需系统性基准测试[9][10]。
> 
> 来源：https://www.nature.com/articles/s41592-025-02772-6
> 来源：https://lifesciencesaihandbook.com/cells/single-cell-models.html

### 2.5 数字孪生：个体化治疗模拟的最前沿

数字孪生（Digital Twin）技术是将大模型/基础模型应用于个体化药物评估的最前沿方向之一。数字孪生本质上是真实患者的虚拟复制品，通过整合个体化医疗数据（基因组、影像、生理监测等），构建高度详细的实时模拟。

**生成式AI驱动的数字孪生**能够预测疾病轨迹并模拟药物治疗效果。这些模型通过在大规模异质数据上训练，有效学习患者诊断、临床变量与结局之间的复杂关系，从而显著增强个体化预测能力[11]。

> **关键事实**：数字孪生模型可模拟药物在不同患者体内的药理学效应和相互作用，实现从“群体平均”到“个体特定”的治疗策略转变[11]。
> 
> 来源：https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/17460441.2025.2507376

在肿瘤学中，“癌症阿凡达”（Cancer Avatar）技术通过整合影像、组织学和基因组数据，允许临床医生在做出治疗决策前虚拟测试不同治疗策略。在放射肿瘤学和免疫治疗中，剂量和时序的个体化调整对疗效和毒性有显著影响[12]。

> **关键事实**：癌症阿凡达技术整合多模态数据，可虚拟测试不同治疗策略，在放射肿瘤学和免疫治疗中具有重要价值[12]。
> 
> 来源：https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12653454

在脊髓性肌萎缩症（SMA）等罕见病中，数字孪生已被用于模拟AAV载体的生物分布和免疫原性，其预测结果与临床试验数据的前瞻性验证相匹配[12]。

**多尺度数字孪生**进一步整合了从分子到细胞、组织、器官乃至整个人群的多个生物尺度，结合机械模型与AI驱动组件，支持靶点验证、先导化合物优化、PK/PD建模和临床试验设计[13]。

> **关键事实**：多尺度数字孪生整合分子到人群多个生物尺度，结合机械模型与AI，支持从靶点验证到临床试验设计的全链条优化[13]。
> 
> 来源：https://www.news-medical.net/life-sciences/Digital-Twins-in-Precision-Medicine-and-Drug-Discovery.aspx

### 2.6 毒性预测与ADMET评估

药物毒性是导致临床试验失败的主要原因之一（约30%的失败率）。AI驱动的毒性预测正从单一终点向多模态整合和生成式AI方向演进[14]。

**AI在预测毒理学中的市场**在2025年已达2.8亿美元，预计到2035年将增长至22.6亿美元（CAGR 23.2%），反映了行业对这一技术的强烈需求[15]。

**多任务学习框架**可同时预测多个毒性终点，整合hERG通道阻断、肝毒性、基因毒性等评估。在基准测试中，AI模型在神经活性干扰（AUROC=0.85）、神经毒性（AUROC=0.83）等任务上表现出良好性能[16]。

> **关键事实**：AI毒性预测模型在多个终点上达到良好性能（如神经毒性AUROC=0.83），但肝毒性预测仍因异质性生物学机制而面临挑战[16]。
> 
> 来源：https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/chemistry/articles/10.3389/fchem.2025.1632046/full

**数字孪生技术**也被应用于动态药物反应模拟，整合多组学数据以提供更全面的安全性评估。未来方向包括通过可解释AI技术增强模型透明度，以及采用混合学习和多任务学习方法[17]。

> **关键事实**：AI毒性预测的未来方向包括可解释AI、多组学数据整合、数字孪生动态模拟以及持续的数据共享机制[17]。
> 
> 来源：https://synapse.patsnap.com/article/how-does-ai-assist-in-the-early-detection-of-drug-toxicity

### 2.7 药物相互作用预测

药物-药物相互作用（DDI）是临床用药安全的重要考量。LLM在这一领域展现出显著优势。

**LLM-DDI**框架利用小规模LLM在DDI预测任务上表现出与大型模型相当甚至更优的性能，具有重要的临床应用意义——无需大量计算资源即可实现可靠的DDI预测[18]。

**基于深度学习的DDI预测**方法已达到约92%的准确率，通过整合CYP450抑制数据、药物-靶点基因关联和分子结构信息，能够识别传统定量构效关系模型难以捕捉的复杂相互作用模式[19]。

> **关键事实**：LLM在DDI预测中展现出与大型模型相当甚至更优的性能，且计算需求更低，更适用于临床部署[18]。
> 
> 来源：https://arxiv.org/pdf/2502.06890

### 2.8 临床药理学教育中的LLM模拟

除直接用于药物评估外，LLM还被用于药理学教育中的患者模拟。一项混合方法评估研究在104名药学博士学生中测试了ChatGPT、Claude、DeepSeek和Gemini生成的急性髓系白血病/慢性髓系白血病模拟病例，系统评估了LLM在生成可扩展的临床模拟方面的教学严谨性和临床可靠性[20]。

> **关键事实**：LLM生成的患者模拟已用于临床药理学教育，在多个LLM平台上进行了系统评估，显示出教学潜力[20]。
> 
> 来源：https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02626-1

## 3. 当前阶段的核心挑战与局限

尽管大模型在药物系统性评估中展现出巨大潜力，但当前阶段仍面临多方面的严峻挑战。

### 3.1 简单基线模型的竞争

如前所述，2024-2025年的多项独立基准测试表明，在单细胞扰动预测等核心任务上，深度基础模型并未持续超越简单的线性方法。这一发现具有重要的方法论意义：在追求模型复杂度的同时，必须建立严格的基线比较体系，确保新方法的性能提升来自于真正的生物学洞察而非过拟合[9][10]。

### 3.2 数据质量、规模与异质性

AI模型的性能高度依赖于训练数据的质量和规模。当前面临的主要数据挑战包括：
- **批次效应与混杂因素**：不同实验室、不同平台产生的组学数据存在系统性偏差，需要强大的批次校正能力。
- **标注稀疏性**：高质量的药物反应标注数据（尤其是在患者层面）极为稀缺。
- **知识更新滞后**：生物医学知识持续快速更新，模型的性能会随着知识老化而下降，评估必须是一个持续的过程而非一次性事件[21]。

> **关键事实**：生物医学知识快速更新，LLM性能会随知识老化而下降，评估应是持续性过程，包括对真实世界输出的监控[21]。
> 
> 来源：https://intuitionlabs.ai/articles/llm-evaluation-biotech-guide

### 3.3 可解释性与幻觉问题

在药物评估这一高风险领域，模型的可解释性至关重要。LLM的“黑箱”性质以及其生成看似合理但实际错误的“幻觉”内容，是临床部署的主要障碍。尽管多模态LLM框架可以整合不同数据类型，但其推理过程仍然缺乏透明性[6]。

### 3.4 个体间异质性的建模困难

尽管大模型在捕捉群体水平模式上表现出色，但在真实世界中，个体间异质性受到众多因素影响——年龄、性别、种族、遗传多态性、代谢组谱、微生物组、环境暴露等。现有模型在泛化到新患者群体时仍面临挑战，尤其是在训练数据代表性不足的人群中[22]。

> **关键事实**：疾病异质性受年龄、性别、种族、遗传等多因素影响，AI模型在泛化到训练数据代表性不足的患者群体时面临挑战，需包容性试验设计[22]。
> 
> 来源：https://www.nature.com/articles/s41392-026-02631-6

### 3.5 监管与验证缺口

尽管FDA已在2025年发布了关于AI支持药物研发决策的指南草案，引入了基于风险的模型可信度框架，强调透明度、验证和数据治理，但AI模型的临床验证和监管整合仍处于早期阶段[23]。

> **关键事实**：FDA在2025年发布AI支持药物研发的指南草案，引入基于风险的模型可信度框架，但AI在药物开发中的可测量影响仍缺乏系统表征[23]。
> 
> 来源：https://www.drugdiscoverynews.com/ai-is-transforming-drug-discovery-16706

## 4. 未来发展方向

### 4.1 多模态LLM代理系统

未来，药物评估将越来越多地依赖能够自主融合多源信息的LLM代理系统。这些系统不仅可以整合结构化分子谱和临床数据，还可以实时检索最新文献、知识图谱和数据库，实现上下文感知的、动态更新的药物评估。在肿瘤学中，这种系统已展示出提供个性化治疗建议的可行性，预计将扩展到更多疾病领域[6]。

### 4.2 大规模扰动模型（Large Perturbation Models）

GSK团队提出的**大规模扰动模型（LPM）** 代表了从“相关性学习”到“因果推断”的转变。传统虚拟细胞模型从单细胞RNA-seq中学习数据间的相关性，即“什么与什么相关”，而非“什么导致什么”。LPM采用不同的方法，通过在多种细胞类型和条件下系统训练扰动数据，学习跨上下文的通用生物学响应规律[24]。

> **关键事实**：LPM从相关性学习转向因果推断，通过在多种细胞类型和条件下训练扰动数据，学习跨上下文的通用生物学响应规律[24]。
> 
> 来源：https://www.linkedin.com/posts/vsavova_deep-learning-based-gene-perturbation-effect-activity-7360314175551639552-mjBK

### 4.3 患者特异性数字孪生

数字孪生技术将从概念验证走向临床整合。未来，每个患者都可能拥有一个持续更新的数字孪生，整合来自基因组学、影像学、可穿戴设备、电子健康记录的多维度数据，实时模拟疾病轨迹和药物反应。在约翰霍普金斯大学，基因型特异性心脏孪生项目已利用MRI和基因组数据创建3D患者心脏复制品，模拟导管消融对室性心动过速的影响[25]。

> **关键事实**：数字孪生技术正从概念走向临床，约翰霍普金斯大学已利用MRI和基因组数据创建患者特异性心脏孪生，模拟治疗干预效果[25]。
> 
> 来源：https://www.nature.com/articles/s41540-025-00592-0

### 4.4 闭环学习：从预测到实验验证再到模型更新

未来药物评估模型将建立“预测-实验-更新”的闭环系统。模型预测药物在特定患者群体中的效果，实验验证关键预测，将验证结果反馈回模型进行持续优化。这种主动学习范式可以显著减少实验次数，加快药物研发周期[7]。

### 4.5 监管科学的发展

随着AI在药物研发中应用的深入，监管框架将逐步成熟。FDA的CDER AI委员会（2024年成立）正在推动AI使用监管方法的协调统一。未来可能形成“AI辅助”与“AI驱动”两种监管路径，前者要求人类专家监督，后者则需要更严格的验证和透明度要求[23]。

### 4.6 从群体平均到个体精准的范式转移

综合来看，大模型正在推动药物评估从“群体平均模型”向“个体化精准模拟”的根本性转变。这一转变的三大支柱是：
1. **多模态数据整合**：基因组、转录组、蛋白质组、代谢组、影像、临床记录的深度融合
2. **因果推断能力**：从相关关系走向因果关系，理解药物作用的生物学机制
3. **持续学习机制**：模型从每次临床反馈中学习，不断优化个体化预测

---

## 5. 结论

**当前阶段，大模型（LLM/基础模型）已经初步具备了模拟药物效应、进行系统性药物评估的能力，但仍处于从“实验室验证”到“临床可部署”的关键过渡期。**

在药物反应预测、多组学整合、单细胞扰动模拟、毒性预测、药物相互作用预测等领域，大模型展现出了超越传统方法的潜力，特别是在处理高维、异构、多模态数据方面具有天然优势。DRPLLM、scGPT、Geneformer、scFoundation等模型在特定任务上取得了令人瞩目的成果，数字孪生技术更是将个体化药物模拟推向了新的高度。

然而，**需要清醒认识到当前阶段的局限性**：在扰动预测等核心任务上，简单基线模型仍有竞争力；个体间异质性的建模仍不完善；模型的可解释性、幻觉问题、数据偏差和监管空白尚未解决。这些挑战决定了短期内大模型不会完全取代传统实验方法，而是作为强力的辅助工具，加速药物研发并提高临床试验成功率。

**未来十年**，随着多模态LLM代理系统、大规模扰动模型、患者特异性数字孪生、闭环学习框架等技术的成熟，以及监管框架的完善和计算基础设施的民主化，大模型有望真正实现“在计算机中模拟药物对每一个体的全部影响”这一终极目标。这将从根本上改变药物研发的范式——从“发现”走向“设计”，从“群体试验”走向“个体模拟”，最终实现真正的精准医学。

## **Webpage Content** 
Title: Deep-learning-based gene perturbation effect prediction does not yet outperform simple linear baselines

URL Source: https://www.nature.com/articles/s41592-025-02772-6

Markdown Content:
*   Brief Communication
*   [Open access](https://www.springernature.com/gp/open-science/about/the-fundamentals-of-open-access-and-open-research)
*   Published: 04 August 2025

*   [Constantin Ahlmann-Eltze](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41592-025-02772-6#auth-Constantin-Ahlmann_Eltze-Aff1-Aff2-Aff3)[ORCID: orcid.org/0000-0002-3762-068X](https://orcid.org/0000-0002-3762-068X)[1](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41592-025-02772-6#Aff1),[2](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41592-025-02772-6#Aff2)[nAff3](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41592-025-02772-6#nAff3), 
*   [Wolfgang Huber](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41592-025-02772-6#auth-Wolfgang-Huber-Aff2)[ORCID: orcid.org/0000-0002-0474-2218](https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0474-2218)[2](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41592-025-02772-6#Aff2)&
*   [Simon Anders](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41592-025-02772-6#auth-Simon-Anders-Aff1)[ORCID: orcid.org/0000-0003-4868-1805](https://orcid.org/0000-0003-4868-1805)[1](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41592-025-02772-6#Aff1)

[_Nature Methods_](https://www.nature.com/nmeth)**volume 22**,pages 1657–1661 (2025) [Cite this article](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41592-025-02772-6#citeas)

*   110k Accesses

*   207 Citations

*   184 Altmetric

*   [Metrics details](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41592-025-02772-6/metrics)

## Abstract

Recent research in deep-learning-based foundation models promises to learn representations of single-cell data that enable prediction of the effects of genetic perturbations. Here we compared five foundation models and two other deep learning models against deliberately simple baselines for predicting transcriptome changes after single or double perturbations. None outperformed the baselines, which highlights the importance of critical benchmarking in directing and evaluating method development.

### Similar content being viewed by others

![Image 1](https://media.springernature.com/w215h120/springer-static/image/art%3A10.1038%2Fs41588-025-02169-3/MediaObjects/41588_2025_2169_Fig1_HTML.png)

![Image 2](https://media.springernature.com/w215h120/springer-static/image/art%3A10.1038%2Fs41598-024-67023-8/MediaObjects/41598_2024_67023_Fig1_HTML.png)

![Image 3](https://media.springernature.com/w215h120/springer-static/image/art%3A10.1038%2Fs41598-026-37483-1/MediaObjects/41598_2026_37483_Fig1_HTML.png)

## Main

The success of large language models in knowledge representation has spawned efforts to apply the foundation model concept to biology[1](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41592-025-02772-6#ref-CR1 "Gavriilidis, G. I., Vasileiou, V., Orfanou, A., Ishaque, N. & Psomopoulos, F. A mini-review on perturbation modelling across single-cell omic modalities. Comput. Struct. Biotechnol. J. 23, 1886 (2024)."),[2](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41592-025-02772-6#ref-CR2 "Szałata, A. et al. Transformers in single-cell omics: a review and new perspectives. Nat. Methods 21, 1430–1443 (2024)."),[3](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41592-025-02772-6#ref-CR3 "Rood, J. E., Hupalowska, A. & Regev, A. Toward a foundation model of causal cell and tissue biology with a perturbation cell and tissue atlas. Cell 187, 4520–4545 (2024)."). Several single-cell foundation models trained on transcriptomics data from millions of single cells have been published[4](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41592-025-02772-6#ref-CR4 "Yang, F. et al. scBERT as a large-scale pretrained deep language model for cell type annotation of single-cell RNA-seq data. Nat. Mach. Intell. 4, 852–866 (2022)."),[5](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41592-025-02772-6#ref-CR5 "Theodoris, C. V. et al. Transfer learning enables predictions in network biology. Nature 618, 616–624 (2023)."),[6](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41592-025-02772-6#ref-CR6 "Rosen, Y. et al. Universal cell embeddings: a foundation model for cell biology. Preprint at bioRxiv 
                  https://doi.org/10.1101/2023.11.28.568918
                  
                 (2023)."). Two recent models—scGPT[7](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41592-025-02772-6#ref-CR7 "Cui, H. et al. scGPT: toward building a foundation model for single-cell multi-omics using generative AI. Nat. Methods 21, 1470–1480 (2024).") and scFoundation[8](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41592-025-02772-6#ref-CR8 "Hao, M. et al. Large-scale foundation model on single-cell transcriptomics. Nat. Methods 21, 1481–1491 (2024).")—claim to be able to predict gene expression changes caused by genetic perturbations.

In the present study, we benchmarked the performance of these models against GEARS[9](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41592-025-02772-6#ref-CR9 "Roohani, Y., Huang, K. & Leskovec, J. Predicting transcriptional outcomes of novel multigene perturbations with GEARS. Nat. Biotechnol. 42, 927–935 (2024).") and CPA[10](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41592-025-02772-6#ref-CR10 "Lotfollahi, M. et al. Predicting cellular responses to complex perturbations in high-throughput screens. Mol. Syst. Biol. 19, e11517 (2023).") and against deliberately simplistic baselines. To provide additional perspective, we also included three single-cell foundation models—scBERT[4](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41592-025-02772-6#ref-CR4 "Yang, F. et al. scBERT as a large-scale pretrained deep language model for cell type annotation of single-cell RNA-seq data. Nat. Mach. Intell. 4, 852–866 (2022)."), Geneformer[5](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41592-025-02772-6#ref-CR5 "Theodoris, C. V. et al. Transfer learning enables predictions in network biology. Nature 618, 616–624 (2023).") and UCE[6](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41592-025-02772-6#ref-CR6 "Rosen, Y. et al. Universal cell embeddings: a foundation model for cell biology. Preprint at bioRxiv 
                  https://doi.org/10.1101/2023.11.28.568918
                  
                 (2023).")—that were not explicitly designed for this task but can be repurposed for it by combining them with a linear decoder that maps the cell embedding to the gene expression space. In the figures, we marked their results with an asterisk.

We first assessed prediction of expression changes after double perturbations. We used data by Norman et al.[11](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41592-025-02772-6#ref-CR11 "Norman, T. M. et al. Exploring genetic interaction manifolds constructed from rich single-cell phenotypes. Science 365, 786–793 (2019)."), in which 100 individual genes and 124 pairs of genes were upregulated in K562 cells with a CRISPR activation system (Extended Data Fig. [1](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41592-025-02772-6#Fig3)). The phenotypes for these 224 perturbations, plus the no-perturbation control, are logarithm-transformed RNA sequencing expression values for 19,264 genes.

We fine-tuned the models on all 100 single perturbations and on 62 of the double perturbations and assessed the prediction error on the remaining 62 double perturbations. For robustness, we ran each analysis five times using different random partitions.

For comparison, we included two simple baselines: (1) the ‘no change’ model that always predicts the same expression as in the control condition and (2) the ‘additive’ model that, for each double perturbation, predicts the sum of the individual logarithmic fold changes (LFCs). Neither uses the double perturbation data.

All models had a prediction error substantially higher than the additive baseline (Fig. [1a,b](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41592-025-02772-6#Fig1)). Here, prediction error is the _L_ 2 distance between predicted and observed expression values for the 1,000 most highly expressed genes. We also examined other summary statistics, such as the Pearson delta measure, and _L_ 2 distances for other gene subsets: the _n_ most highly expressed or the _n_ most differentially expressed genes, for various _n_. We got the same overall result (Extended Data Fig. [2](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41592-025-02772-6#Fig4)).

**Fig. 1: Double perturbation prediction.**

**a**, Beeswarm plot of the prediction errors for 62 double perturbations across five test–training splits. The prediction error is measured by the _L_ 2 distance between the predicted and the observed expression profile of the _n_ = 1,000 most highly expressed genes. The horizontal red lines show the mean per model, which, for the best-performing model, is extended by the dashed line. **b**, Scatterplots of observed versus predicted expression from one example of the 62 double perturbations. The numbers indicate error measured by the _L_ 2 distance and the Pearson delta (_R_ 2). **c**, TPR (recall) of the interaction predictions as a function of the false discovery proportion. FN, false negative; FP, false positive; TP, true positive. **d**, Schematic of the classification of interactions based on the difference from the additive expectation (the error bars show the additive range). **e**, Bar chart of the composition of the observed interaction classes. **f**, Top: scatterplot of observed versus predicted expression compared to the additive expectation. Each point is one of the 1,000 read-out genes under one of the 62 double perturbations across five test–training splits. The 500 predictions that deviated most from the additive expectation are depicted with bigger and more saturated points. Bottom: mosaic plots that compare the composition of highlighted predictions from the top panel stratified by the interaction class of the prediction. The width of the bars is scaled to match the number of instances. Source data for Fig. 1 are provided. expr., expression.

[Source data](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41592-025-02772-6#MOESM3)

Next, we considered the ability of the models to predict genetic interactions. Conceptually, a genetic interaction exists if the phenotype of two (or more) simultaneous perturbations is ‘surprising’. We operationalized this as double perturbation phenotypes that differed from the additive expectation more than expected under a null model with a Normal distribution (Extended Data Fig. [3](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41592-025-02772-6#Fig5) and [Methods](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41592-025-02772-6#Sec2)). Using the full dataset, we identified 5,035 genetic interactions (out of potentially 124,000) at a false discovery rate of 5%.

We then obtained genetic interaction predictions from each model by computing, for each of its 310,000 predictions (1,000 read-out genes and 62 held-out double perturbations across five test–training splits), the difference between predicted expression and additive expectation, and, if that difference exceeded a given threshold _D_, we called a predicted interaction. We then computed, for all possible choices of _D_, the true-positive rate (TPR) and the false discovery proportion, which resulted in the curves shown in Fig. [1c](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41592-025-02772-6#Fig1). The additive model did not compete as, by definition, it does not predict interactions.

None of the models was better than the ‘no change’ baseline. The same ranking of models was observed when using other metrics (Extended Data Fig. [4](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41592-025-02772-6#Fig6)).

To further dissect this finding, we classified the interactions as ‘buffering’, ‘synergistic’ or ‘opposite’ (Fig. [1d,e](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41592-025-02772-6#Fig1) and [Methods](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41592-025-02772-6#Sec2)). All models mostly predicted buffering interactions. The ‘no change’ baseline cannot, by definition, find synergistic interactions, but also the deep learning models rarely predicted synergistic interactions, and it was even rarer that those predictions were correct (Fig. [1f](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41592-025-02772-6#Fig1)).

To our surprise, we often found the same pair of hemoglobin genes (_HBG2_ and _HBZ_) among the top predicted interactions, across models and double perturbations (Extended Data Fig. [5](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41592-025-02772-6#Fig7)). Examining the data, we noted that all models except Geneformer and scFoundation predicted LFC ≈ 0—like the ‘no change’ baseline—for the double perturbation of these two genes, despite their strong individual effects (Extended Data Fig. [6](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41592-025-02772-6#Fig8)). More generally, we noted that, for most genes, the predictions of scGPT, UCE and scBERT did not vary across perturbations, and those of GEARS and scFoundation varied considerably less than the ground truth (Extended Data Fig. [7](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41592-025-02772-6#Fig9)).

GEARS, scGPT and scFoundation also claim the ability to predict the effect of unseen perturbations. GEARS uses shared Gene Ontology[12](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41592-025-02772-6#ref-CR12 "The Gene Ontology Consortium. The Gene Ontology knowledgebase in 2023. Genetics 224, iyad031 (2023).") annotations to extrapolate from the training data, whereas the foundation models are supposed to have learned the relationships between genes during pretraining to predict unseen perturbations.

To benchmark this functionality, we used two CRISPR interference datasets by Replogle et al.[13](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41592-025-02772-6#ref-CR13 "Replogle, J. M. et al. Mapping information-rich genotype-phenotype landscapes with genome-scale Perturb-seq. Cell 185, 2559–2575 (2022).") obtained with K562 and RPE1 cells and a dataset by Adamson et al.[14](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41592-025-02772-6#ref-CR14 "Adamson, B. et al. A multiplexed single-cell CRISPR screening platform enables systematic dissection of the unfolded protein response. Cell 167, 1867–1882 (2016).") obtained with K562 cells (Extended Data Fig. [1](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41592-025-02772-6#Fig3)).

As a baseline, we devised a simple linear model. It represents each read-out gene with a _K_-dimensional vector and each perturbation with an _L_-dimensional vector. These vectors are collected in the matrices **G**, with one row per read-out gene, and **P**, with one row per perturbation. **G** and **P** are either obtained as dimension-reducing embeddings of the training data ([Methods](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41592-025-02772-6#Sec2)) or provided by an external source (see below). Then, given a data matrix **Y**train of gene expression values, with one row per read-out gene and one column per perturbation (that is, per condition pseudobulk of the single-cell data), the _K_ × _L_ matrix **W** is found as

$$\mathop{{\rm{argmin}}}\limits_{{\bf{W}}}| | {{\bf{Y}}}_{{\rm{train}}}-({\bf{G}}{\bf{W}}{{\bf{P}}}^{T}+{\boldsymbol{b}})| {| }_{2}^{2},$$

(1)

where **_b_** is the vector of row means of **Y**train (Fig. [2b](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41592-025-02772-6#Fig2)).

**Fig. 2: Single perturbation prediction.**

**a**, Beeswarm plot of the prediction errors for 134, 210 and 24 unseen single perturbations across two test–training splits ([Methods](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41592-025-02772-6#Sec2)). The prediction error is measured by the _L_ 2 distance between the mean predicted and observed expression profile of the _n_ = 1,000 most highly expressed genes. The horizontal red lines show the mean per model, which, for the best-performing model, is extended by the dashed line. DL, deep learning; LM, linear model. **b**, Schematic of the LM and how it can accommodate available gene (**G**) or perturbation (**P**) embeddings. **c**, Forest plot comparing the performance of all models relative to the error of the ‘mean’ baseline. The point ranges show the overall mean and 95% confidence interval of the bootstrapped mean ratio between each model and the baseline for 134, 210 and 24 unseen single perturbations across two test–training splits. The opacity of the point range is reduced if the confidence interval contains 0. Source data for Fig. 2 are provided.

[Source data](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41592-025-02772-6#MOESM4)

We also included an even simpler baseline, **_b_**, the mean across the perturbations in the training set, following the preprints by Kernfeld et al.[15](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41592-025-02772-6#ref-CR15 "Kernfeld, E., Yang, Y., Weinstock, J. S., Battle, A. & Cahan, P. A systematic comparison of computational methods for expression forecasting. Preprint at bioRxiv 
                  https://doi.org/10.1101/2023.07.28.551039
                  
                 (2024).") and Csendes et al.[16](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41592-025-02772-6#ref-CR16 "Csendes, G., Sanz, G., Szalay, K. Z. & Szalai, B. Benchmarking foundation cell models for post-perturbation RNA-seq prediction. BMC Genomics 26, 393 (2025).") that appeared while this paper was in revision.

None of the deep learning models was able to consistently outperform the mean prediction or the linear model (Fig. [2a](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41592-025-02772-6#Fig2) and Extended Data Fig. [8](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41592-025-02772-6#Fig10)). We did not include scFoundation in this benchmark, as it required each dataset to exactly match the genes from its own pretraining data, and, for the Adamson and Replogle data, most of the required genes were missing. We also did not include CPA, as it is not designed to predict the effects of unseen perturbations.

Next, we asked whether we could find utility in the data representations that GEARS, scGPT and scFoundation had learned during their pretraining. We extracted a gene embedding matrix **G** from scFoundation and scGPT, respectively, and a perturbation embedding matrix **P** from GEARS. The above linear model, equipped with these embeddings, performed as well or better than scGPT and GEARS with their in-built decoders (Fig. [2c](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41592-025-02772-6#Fig2)). Furthermore, the linear models with the gene embeddings from scFoundation and scGPT outperformed the ‘mean’ baseline, but they did not consistently outperform the linear model using **G** and **P** from the training data.

The approach that did consistently outperform all other models was a linear model with **P** pretrained on the Replogle data (using the K562 cell line data as pretraining for the Adamson and RPE1 data and the RPE1 cell line for the K562 data). The predictions were more accurate for genes that were more similar between K562 and RPE1 (Extended Data Fig. [9](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41592-025-02772-6#Fig11)). Together, these results suggest that pretraining on the single-cell atlas data provided only a small benefit over random embeddings, but pretraining on perturbation data increased predictive performance.

In summary, we presented prediction tasks where current foundation models did not perform better than deliberately simplistic linear prediction models, despite significant computational expenses for fine-tuning the deep learning models (Extended Data Fig. [10](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41592-025-02772-6#Fig12)). As our deliberately simple baselines are incapable of representing realistic biological complexity, yet were not outperformed by the foundation models, we conclude that the latter’s goal of providing a generalizable representation of cellular states and predicting the outcome of not-yet-performed experiments is still elusive.

The publications that presented GEARS, scGPT and scFoundation included comparisons against GEARS and CPA and against a linear model. Some of these comparisons may have happened to be particularly ‘easy’. For instance, CPA was never designed to predict effects of unseen perturbations and was particularly uncompetitive in the double perturbation benchmark. The linear model used in scGPT’s benchmark appears to have been set up such that it reverts to predicting no change over the control condition for any unseen perturbation.

Our results are in line with previously published benchmarks that assessed the performance of foundation models for other tasks and found negligible benefits compared to simpler approaches[17](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41592-025-02772-6#ref-CR17 "Kedzierska, K. Z., Crawford, L., Amini, A. P. & Lu, A. X. Zero-shot evaluation reveals limitations of single-cell foundation models. Genome Biol. 26, 101 (2025)."),[18](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41592-025-02772-6#ref-CR18 "Boiarsky, R., Singh, N., Buendia, A., Getz, G. & Sontag, D. A deep dive into single-cell RNA sequencing foundation models. Preprint at bioRxiv 
                  https://doi.org/10.1101/2023.10.19.563100
                  
                 (2023)."),[19](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41592-025-02772-6#ref-CR19 "Liu, T., Li, K., Wang, Y., Li, H. & Zhao, H. Evaluating the utilities of foundation models in single-cell data analysis. Preprint at bioRxiv 
                  https://doi.org/10.1101/2023.09.08.555192
                  
                 (2024)."). Our results also concur with two previous studies showing that simple baselines outperform GEARS for predicting unseen single or double perturbations[20](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41592-025-02772-6#ref-CR20 "Märtens, K., Donovan-Maiye, R. & Ferkinghoff-Borg, J. Enhancing generative perturbation models with LLM-informed gene embeddings. In Proc. Workshop on Machine Learning for Genomics Explorations (ICLR, 2024). 
                  https://openreview.net/forum?id=eb3ndUlkt4
                  
                "),[21](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41592-025-02772-6#ref-CR21 "Gaudelet, T. et al. Season combinatorial intervention predictions with salt & peper. In Proc. Workshop on Machine Learning for Genomics Explorations (ICLR, 2024). 
                  https://openreview.net/forum?id=Wj95feICkN
                  
                "). Since the release of our paper as a preprint, several other benchmarks[15](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41592-025-02772-6#ref-CR15 "Kernfeld, E., Yang, Y., Weinstock, J. S., Battle, A. & Cahan, P. A systematic comparison of computational methods for expression forecasting. Preprint at bioRxiv 
                  https://doi.org/10.1101/2023.07.28.551039
                  
                 (2024)."),[16](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41592-025-02772-6#ref-CR16 "Csendes, G., Sanz, G., Szalay, K. Z. & Szalai, B. One limitation of our benchmark is that we used only four datasets. We chose these as they were used in the publications presenting GEARS, scGPT and scFoundation. Another limitation is that all datasets are from cancer cell lines, which, for example, Theodoris et al.[5](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41592-025-02772-6#ref-CR5 "Theodoris, C. V. et al. Transfer learning enables predictions in network biology. Nature 618, 616–624 (2023).") excluded from their training data because of concerns about their high mutational burden. We also did not attempt to improve the original quality control, for example, by excluding perturbations that did not affect the expression of their own target gene and, thus, might not have worked as intended.

Deep learning is effective in many areas of single-cell omics[28](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41592-025-02772-6#ref-CR28 "Gayoso, A. et al. However, prediction of perturbation effects still remains an open challenge, as our present work shows. We expect that increased focus on performance metrics and benchmarking will be instrumental to facilitate eventual success in applying transfer learning to perturbation data.

## Methods

### Data

We ran the double perturbation benchmark on the data produced by Norman et al.[11](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41592-025-02772-6#ref-CR11 "Norman, T. M. et al. Exploring genetic interaction manifolds constructed from rich single-cell phenotypes. Science 365, 786–793 (2019).") and reprocessed by scFoundation. For the single gene perturbation benchmarks, we used the data from Adamson et al.[14](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41592-025-02772-6#ref-CR14 "Adamson, B. et al. A multiplexed single-cell CRISPR screening platform enables systematic dissection of the unfolded protein response. Cell 167, 1867–1882 (2016).") and Replogle et al.[13](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41592-025-02772-6#ref-CR13 "Replogle, J. M. et al. Mapping information-rich genotype-phenotype landscapes with genome-scale Perturb-seq. Cell 185, 2559–2575 (2022).") as provided by GEARS (details in ‘Data availability’).

### Software versions and parameters

We ran GEARS version 0.1.2, scGPT version 0.2.1, scFoundation (which is built on top of a GEARS version 0.0.2 fork), CPA version 0.8.8, Geneformer version 0.1.0, scBERT from commit hash 262fd4b9 with model weights provided by the authors and UCE at commit hash 8227a65c. We used each model, as much as possible, with their default parameters. All scripts that were used to predict the expression changes are available on GitHub ([https://github.com/const-ae/linear_perturbation_prediction-Paper/tree/main/benchmark/src](https://github.com/const-ae/linear_perturbation_prediction-Paper/tree/main/benchmark/src)).

*   GEARS and scFoundation provide a straightforward application programming interface (API) to predict the expression change after perturbation. We limited the fine-tuning time to 3 days, which meant that we trained scFoundation for five epochs.

*   For scGPT, we used the same parameters and code as in their [tutorial](https://scgpt.readthedocs.io/en/v0.2.1/tutorial_perturbation.html) for perturbation prediction.

*   For CPA, we used the code from their [tutorial](https://cpa-tools.readthedocs.io/en/latest/tutorials/Norman.html) on how to predict combinatorial CRISPR perturbations on the Norman dataset.

*   For Geneformer, we fine-tuned the provided model by predicting the perturbation labels of the training data. We then used the built-in in silico perturbation functionality to calculate the perturbed embedding.

*   UCE is designed for zero-shot use, which means that it does not need to be fine-tuned. We report results from the four-layer version of UCE (as we found no performance difference between the four-layer and 33-layer versions). UCE does not provide functionality for in silico perturbation, so we calculated the post-perturbation embedding by taking the expression matrix for the unperturbed cells and overwrote the rows for the genes that we wanted to perturb with the values from the ground truth expression matrix. We, thus, tried to ensure that we tested the model under the best conditions, accepting that test data leakage could theoretically give the model an advantage over the other models.

*   We fine-tuned scBERT on predicting the perturbation labels of the training data. We then used the same approach to calculate the embedding after in silico perturbation that we used for UCE.

To predict the expression changes from the embeddings of Geneformer, UCE and scBERT, we added a linear decoder to the models. We fitted a ridge regression model that predicted the gene expression of the perturbed cells from the perturbed embeddings of the training data. We then used that ridge regression to predict the gene expression of the test data from the corresponding perturbed embeddings and continued with the mean of the predicted values per perturbation.

To reduce the probability that we understate the performance for any of the models, due to wrong or suboptimal operation by ourselves, we reached out to the original authors of the benchmarked models and asked them to review our code. The authors of CPA perceived a problem with our code and submitted a [fix](https://github.com/const-ae/linear_perturbation_prediction-Paper/pull/3); however, as the new code had worse performance than the original version, here we report results of the original code.

### Double perturbation benchmark setup

For the double perturbation benchmark, we split the data into test and training sets. We assigned all single-gene perturbations and a randomly chosen half of the double perturbations to the training set and used the other half of the double perturbations as the test set. To reduce stochastic effects on our results, we repeated the whole procedure, including the random test–training splitting, five times.

We used two baseline models: ‘no change’ and ‘additive’. The ‘no change’ model ‘predicted’, for each double perturbation, the expression values seen in the control condition (\({{\boldsymbol{y}}}^{\varnothing }\)). The ‘additive’ model predicts the expression after a double perturbation of genes A and B as

$${\hat{{\boldsymbol{y}}}}^{{\rm{add}}}={{\boldsymbol{y}}}^{\,A}+{{\boldsymbol{y}}}^{B}-{{\boldsymbol{y}}}^{\varnothing },$$

(2)

where **_y_**_A_ and **_y_**_B_ are the mean observed expression vectors for the single perturbation of genes A and B, respectively.

We defined genetic interactions as follows. For each of the 124 double perturbations and the 1,000 read-out genes, we computed the difference between the observed expression value and the additive expectation. These values showed a mixture distribution composed of a large component with a single narrow peak around 0 (corresponding to a majority of non-interactions) and a smaller component consisting of two pronounced tails on either side (corresponding to interactions) (Extended Data Fig. [3](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41592-025-02772-6#Fig5)). To decompose this mixture, we used Efron’s empirical null approach[30](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41592-025-02772-6#ref-CR30 "Efron, B. Large-Scale Inference: Empirical Bayes Methods for Estimation, Testing, and Prediction, Vol. 1 (Cambridge Univ. Press, 2012)."), as implemented in the ‘locfdr’ package (version 1.1-8).

We further classified the interactions, if the two individual LFCs had the same sign, as:

*   ‘buffering’, if the LFC was between 0 and the additive expectation

*   ‘synergistic’, if it exceeded the additive expectation

*   ‘opposite’, if its sign differed from that of the individual perturbations

If the individual effects were in opposite directions, ‘other’. According to this classification, 2.3% of the read-out gene expression values across all double perturbation were buffering interactions; 0.6% were synergistic; and zero were in the opposite direction of the individual perturbations.

### Single perturbation benchmark setup

For the single perturbation benchmark, we used the data as provided by GEARS and also used its ‘simulation’ test–training splitting procedure, which we repeated twice.

To predict the effects of unseen single perturbations, we used two baselines. The ‘mean’ model calculated the mean of the expression values in the training data. The ‘linear model’ is implied in equation ([1](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41592-025-02772-6#Equ1)). We set **_b_** to the row means of the training data (\({\boldsymbol{b}}=1/N{\sum }_{i}{{\bf{Y}}}_{:i}^{{\rm{train}}}\)). We find **G** and **P** as follows. Perform a principal component analysis (PCA) on **Y**train and use the top _K_ principal components for **G**. Then, subset this **G** to only the rows corresponding to genes that were perturbed in the training data (and, hence, appear as columns in **Y**train) and use the resulting matrix for **P**.

Then, we find **W** using the normal equations

$${\bf{W}}={({{\bf{G}}}^{T}{\bf{G}}+\lambda {\bf{I}})}^{-1}{{\bf{G}}}^{T}({{\bf{Y}}}_{{\rm{train}}}-{\boldsymbol{b}}){\bf{P}}{({{\bf{P}}}^{T}{\bf{P}}+\lambda {\bf{I}})}^{-1},$$

(3)

where we use a ridge penalty of _λ_ = 0.1 for numerical stability. Having found a **W**, we can use it for prediction, \(\hat{{\bf{Y}}}={\bf{G}}{\bf{W}}{\tilde{{\bf{P}}}}^{T}+{\boldsymbol{b}}\), where now \(\tilde{{\bf{P}}}\) is the matrix formed by the rows of **G** corresponding to genes perturbed in the test data.

For the single perturbation analysis, not all models were able to predict the expression change for all unseen perturbations. For example, the linear model with **G** and \(\tilde{{\bf{P}}}\) from the training data could only predict perturbations where the target genes were also part of the read-out genes. To evaluate all models on a consistent set of perturbations, we restricted our analysis to those perturbations for which we had predictions from all models (73 perturbations for Adamson, 398 for Replogle K562 and 629 for Replogle RPE1).

We converted GEARS’ Gene Ontology annotations into a perturbation embedding **P** by computing a spectral embedding[31](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41592-025-02772-6#ref-CR31 "Sussman, D. L., Tang, M., Fishkind, D. E. & Priebe, C. E. A consistent adjacency spectral embedding for stochastic blockmodel graphs. J. Am. Stat. Assoc. 107, 1119–1128 (2012)."),[32](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41592-025-02772-6#ref-CR32 "Csárdi, G. & Nepusz, T. The igraph software package for complex network research. InterJournal 1695, 1–9 (2006).") of the pathway membership matrix. We extracted the gene embedding **G** from scGPT following their tutorial on gene regulatory inference. For scFoundation, we extract **G** directly from the pretrained model weights (‘pos_emb.weight’). For the linear model with **P** from the Replogle data, we fitted a 10-dimensional PCA on the columns of the matrix with the perturbation means of the reference data. We fitted all linear models as described in the main text with _K_ = 10; if **G** or **P** was provided, we simply replaced the estimate from the training data with the provided matrix before calculating **W**.

The additive model is a special case of the linear model (equation ([1](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41592-025-02772-6#Equ1))) where the gene embedding is simply the single perturbation data, without any further transformation or dimension reduction (**G** = **Y**single); the perturbation embedding **P** is a binary coding, where each column vector has 1s in the rows of the perturbed genes and is 0 otherwise; and _W_ is an identity matrix and \({\boldsymbol{b}}=-{{\boldsymbol{y}}}^{\varnothing }\).

### Evaluation metrics

We measured the prediction error using the distance \({L}_{2}(\,\hat{{\boldsymbol{y}}},{\boldsymbol{y}})\)\(=\sqrt{{\sum}_{g}{(\,{\hat{y}}_{g}-{y}_{g})}^{2}}\) (also called root mean squared error) between the observed expression values and predictions for the 1,000 most highly expressed genes in the control condition. We also calculated the Pearson delta correlation metric, as suggested by Cui et al.[7](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41592-025-02772-6#ref-CR7 "Cui, H. et al. scGPT: toward building a foundation model for single-cell multi-omics using generative AI. Nat. Methods 21, 1470–1480 (2024)."): \(\mathrm{PearsonDelta}\,(\,\hat{{\boldsymbol{y}}},{\boldsymbol{y}})=\mathrm{cor}\,(\,\hat{{\boldsymbol{y}}}-{{\boldsymbol{y}}}^{\varnothing },{\boldsymbol{y}}-{{\boldsymbol{y}}}^{\varnothing })\). Unlike the _L_ 2 distance, the Pearson delta metric does not penalize predictions that are consistently too small or too large in amplitude and, thus, prioritizes correct prediction of the direction of the expression change.

For the double perturbation data, we assess the TPR (recall) as a function of the false discovery rate. First, we find the order statistic of absolute difference of predictions and additive expectation across all test perturbations (\({\boldsymbol{j}}=\mathrm{argsort}\,(\mathrm{abs}\,(\hat{{\bf{Y}}}-{\hat{{\bf{Y}}}}^{{\rm{add}}}))\)), where \(\hat{{\bf{Y}}}\) is the matrix of the predictions for all genes and perturbations and \({\hat{{\bf{Y}}}}^{{\rm{add}}}\) are the additive expectations.

The false discovery proportion (FDP) at position _l_ ∈ {1, ⋯ , _N_} for a threshold _u_, which separates the interactions from the non-interactions, is

$${{\rm{FDP}}}_{l}=\frac{\mathop{\sum }\nolimits_{i = 1}^{l}{\boldsymbol{1}}(\mathrm{abs}\,{({\bf{Y}}-{\hat{{\bf{Y}}}}^{{\rm{add}}})}_{{{\boldsymbol{j}}}_{i}} < u)}{l}$$

(4)

and the TPR is

$${{\rm{TPR}}}_{l}=\frac{\mathop{\sum }\nolimits_{i = 1}^{l}{\boldsymbol{1}}(\mathrm{abs}\,{({\bf{Y}}-{\hat{{\bf{Y}}}}^{{\rm{add}}})}_{{{\boldsymbol{j}}}_{i}}\ge u)}{\mathop{\sum }\nolimits_{i = 1}^{N}{\boldsymbol{1}}(\mathrm{abs}\,{({\bf{Y}}-{\hat{{\bf{Y}}}}^{{\rm{add}}})}_{i}\ge u)},$$

(5)

where **Y** is the matrix of observed value and _N_ is the product of the number of genes and perturbations. The indicator function **_1_**( ⋅ ) counts how often the observed values **Y** deviate enough from the additive expectation so that the observations are considered an interaction. The order statistic **_j_** ensures that we consider the gene–perturbation pairs first, where the model prediction deviates most from the additive expectation.

Lastly, we find the order statistic of the FDPs (**_s_** = argsort(FDP)) and plot the tuples 1, ⋯ , _N_

$$({{\rm{FDP}}}_{{{\boldsymbol{s}}}_{l}},{\max }_{i}^{1\cdots l}({{\rm{TPR}}}_{{{\boldsymbol{s}}}_{i}})).$$

(6)

An advantage of considering here the false discovery versus true-positive curve, compared with the precision-recall or the receiver operator curve, is that it provides a direct assessment of which fraction of interactions a model identifies for a fixed fraction of false positives.

(**a**) The Pearson delta measure calculates the correlation of the prediction and observations after subtracting the expression in the control condition. The correlation for the _no change_ predictions could not be calculated because they were all zero. The horizontal red lines show the mean per model, and the dashed line indicates the correlation of the best-performing model. (**b**) Prediction error as a function of _n_, the number of read-out genes. Values under the curve are grey, and the black bars show the observations that exceed what we would expect under the null model. The vertical bar shows the upper and lower thresholds for which the observations have a false discovery rate of less than 5% (that is, the grey fraction of the bars outside the vertical lines is 5%). {
  "rationale": "The user's goal is to extract concrete findings about LLM/foundation model capabilities for drug effect simulation, perturbation prediction, pharmacotherapy simulation, and digital twin personalized therapy. The provided webpage content is a highly relevant, peer-reviewed benchmark study (Nature Methods, 2025) that directly evaluates the performance of several state-of-the-art single-cell foundation models (e.g., scGPT, scFoundation, GEARS, etc.) on the task of predicting gene expression changes following genetic perturbations.   "evidence": "Here we compared five foundation models and two other deep learning models against deliberately simple baselines for predicting transcriptome changes after single or double perturbations. None outperformed the baselines, which highlights the importance of critical benchmarking in directing and evaluating method development.

All models had a prediction error substantially higher than the additive baseline (Fig. 1a,b).

None of the models was better than the ‘no change’ baseline.

None of the deep learning models was able to consistently outperform the mean prediction or the linear model (Fig. 2a and Extended Data Fig. 8).

In summary, we presented prediction tasks where current foundation models did not perform better than deliberately simplistic linear prediction models, despite significant computational expenses for fine-tuning the deep learning models (Extended Data Fig. 10). As our deliberately simple baselines are incapable of representing realistic biological complexity, yet were not outperformed by the foundation models, we conclude that the latter’s goal of providing a generalizable representation of cellular states and predicting the outcome of not-yet-performed experiments is still elusive.

The approach that did consistently outperform all other models was a linear model with P pretrained on the Replogle data... pretraining on the single-cell atlas data provided only a small benefit over random embeddings, but pretraining on perturbation data increased predictive performance.

## **Webpage Content** 
Title: Deep-learning-based gene perturbation effect prediction does not yet outperform simple linear baselines

URL Source: https://www.nature.com/articles/s41592-025-02772-6

Markdown Content:

*   [Constantin Ahlmann-Eltze](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41592-025-02772-6#auth-Constantin-Ahlmann_Eltze-Aff1-Aff2-Aff3)[ORCID: orcid.org/0000-0002-3762-068X](https://orcid.org/0000-0002-3762-068X)[1](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41592-025-02772-6#Aff1),[2](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41592-025-02772-6#Aff2)[nAff3](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41592-025-02772-6#nAff3),

## Abstract

Recent research in deep-learning-based foundation models promises to learn representations of single-cell data that enable prediction of the effects of genetic perturbations. Here we compared five foundation models and two other deep learning models against deliberately simple baselines for predicting transcriptome changes after single or double perturbations. None outperformed the baselines, which highlights the importance of critical benchmarking in directing and evaluating method development.
